articles.title: Philips air purifiers claimed to record up to 98.8% PM2.5 reduction in tests at over 2,000 AQI
articles.summary: Consumer electronics brand Philips has achieved a significant milestone.
articles.body: Consumer electronics brand Philips has achieved a significant milestone. The company has become India's first air purifier brand to have its products independently evaluated under extreme particulate conditions simulating pollution levels exceeding 2,000 AQI. The evaluation, conducted by FARE Labs, a NABL-accredited testing laboratory, recorded up to 98.8% reduction in PM2.5 levels across the Philips air purifier models tested. The tests commenced at an initial monitor-displayed Air Quality Index (AQI) of 2,361.The evaluation covered seven Philips air purifier models across its portfolio: the Philips 4200 Series, 3200 Series, 2200 Series, 1000 Series, 900 Series, 3400 Series (2-in-1 Air Purifier and Humidifier) and 8000 Series (3-in-1). The tests were conducted in a controlled indoor environment with reference to IS 17531:2021, the Bureau of Indian Standards specification for portable indoor air purifiers. Air quality readings were recorded at approximately 30-second intervals.Among the models evaluated, the Philips 4200 Series recorded a 98.8% reduction in PM2.5, with levels declining from 999 µg/m³ to 12 µg/m³ in approximately 21 minutes. PM10 levels reduced by 97.9%, from 1,999 µg/m³ to 42 µg/m³, while the monitor-displayed AQI decreased from 2,361 to 42. The Philips 3400 Series, a 2-in-1 Air Purifier and Humidifier, recorded a 98.5% reduction in PM2.5, with levels declining from 999 µg/m³ to 15 µg/m³. PM10 levels reduced by 97.9%, from 1,999 µg/m³ to 42 µg/m³, while the monitor-displayed AQI decreased from 2,361 to 42 over approximately 32 minutes. The Philips 900 Series recorded a 97.2% reduction in PM2.5, from 999 µg/m³ to 28 µg/m³, alongside a 96.5% reduction in PM10, from 1,999 µg/m³ to 69 µg/m³. The monitor-displayed AQI fell from 2,361 to 68 over approximately 25 minutes. The other models evaluated, including the Philips 3200 Series, 2200 Series, 1000 Series and 8000 Series (3-in-1), also recorded reductions in airborne particulate levels during their respective testing periods.Gulbahar Taurani, MD & CEO, Versuni India, said: "At Versuni, we believe in turning houses into homes, creating spaces where families feel safe, comfortable and cared for. And the air we breathe plays a vital role in making that possible. As India’s No. 1 Air Purifier Brand, we see this as a responsibility that goes beyond just selling products. India is different. Our pollution levels are different, and so are the homes we live in. That is why we believe our air purifiers must not only meet global standards but also prove their performance under the harsh pollution conditions we face in India. Our recent independent evaluation by FARE Labs, conducted under extremely high particulate pollution conditions at over 2,000 AQI, reinforces this commitment. It marks an important milestone in our journey to establish Philips as India’s first air purifier brand Tested for Indian Conditions."C.S. Joshi, Director, FARE Labs, said: “Testing air purifiers under very high pollution levels helps measure how much airborne particulate matter they can remove under controlled conditions. The results provide useful data on their performance during the test. However, results at home may differ depending on factors such as room size, ventilation and other sources of pollution.”Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: Delhi HC clarifies restaurants have no interim relief to levy mandatory service charges
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi high court on Thursday clarified that it has not granted any interim relief to restaurants allowing them to continue charging mandatory
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi high court on Thursday clarified that it has not granted any interim relief to restaurants allowing them to continue charging mandatory service charges from customers, despite an earlier judgment declaring the practice illegal.A Division Bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma said no interim protection had been granted to restaurant associations against the March 28, 2025, judgment of a single judge, which upheld the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) guidelines prohibiting compulsory service charges.The clarification came after Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, appearing for the government told the court that some restaurants were still making service charges mandatory for customers, contrary to the High Court's earlier ruling, ANI reported.Sharma submitted that restaurants could not continue the practice after the single judge had upheld the CCPA guidelines prohibiting hotels and restaurants from automatically adding service charges to food bills.Responding to the submission, the bench said it had not granted any interim relief to the restaurant associations in their appeals."Where is the interim relief? Where is the interim relief in their favour? We have not granted any interim prayer," Acting Chief Justice Sambre remarked.The court was hearing appeals filed by the National Restaurant Association of India (NRAI) and the Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Associations of India (FHRAI) against the single judge's March 2025 judgment.What the 2025 judgment saidOn March 28, 2025, Justice Prathiba M Singh dismissed petitions filed by NRAI and FHRAI challenging the CCPA guidelines issued on July 4, 2022.The single judge ruled that restaurants cannot make service charges compulsory, even if they are mentioned on menus. Customers cannot be forced to pay such charges, which must remain voluntary.The court held that collecting service charges without a customer's consent amounts to an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. It also upheld the CCPA's authority to issue guidelines to protect consumer rights and prevent unfair trade practices, imposing costs of Rs 1 lakh on the restaurant associations.The judgment further said restaurants cannot automatically add service charges to bills. Customers must be informed that any additional payment towards service or staff welfare is voluntary.The single judge had also expressed concern over the use of the term 'service charge', observing that it could mislead customers into believing it was a government-imposed tax.Why restaurant associations challenged the banIn their appeals, NRAI and FHRAI argued that collecting service charges was a practice followed by the hospitality industry for more than 80 years and should not be treated as an unfair trade practice.NRAI contended that restaurants which clearly disclose service charges on their menus and inform customers before they place orders should be allowed to collect them.The association argued that service charges are not merely additional earnings for restaurants but are distributed among employees, including waiters, kitchen staff and other workers. It said the system also ensures that employees who do not directly interact with customers receive a share of the collection.The restaurant associations questioned whether the issue should be governed by consumer protection laws or labour laws, particularly when charges are clearly disclosed to customers.They also referred to judicial decisions, labour settlements and wage-related arrangements recognising service charges, including the Supreme Court's 1964 judgment in Management of Wenger & Co. v. Their Workmen.The CCPA issued guidelines on July 4, 2022, prohibiting hotels and restaurants from automatically adding service charges to food bills.The move followed consumer complaints that establishments were adding charges, generally ranging from 5% to 20%, without seeking customers' consent.NRAI approached the Delhi HC on July 18, 2022, challenging the guidelines. FHRAI later filed a separate petition raising similar objections.On July 20, 2022, the High Court stayed the operation of the CCPA guidelines while issuing notices on the petitions.The restaurant associations argued that the guidelines were arbitrary and would adversely affect the hospitality industry. They maintained that service charges were an established practice and helped ensure fair distribution of earnings among restaurant employees.They also pointed out that similar charges were collected in several countries, including the United Kingdom, Singapore, Japan and the United States.However, in March 2025, the single judge rejected their arguments and upheld the CCPA guidelines, ruling that restaurants cannot force customers to pay service charges. The associations have now challenged that decision before the Division Bench.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Indian-origin Samit Patel charged with attempted murder after strangling Uber driver, crushing him with car in Minnesota
articles.summary: Samit Patel, a 25-year-old Indian-origin man, has been charged with attempted murder and carjacking after an brutal assault on Uber driver Mohamed Yusuf, leaving him critically injured in Minnesota.
articles.body: An Indian-origin man has been charged with attempted murder and carjacking in Minnesota after allegedly attacking an Uber driver, strangling him with a seatbelt and running him over with his own vehicle.Samit Apurva Patel, 25, who lives in Hopkins, faces charges of attempted second-degree murder and first-degree carjacking following the Saturday assault on Mohamed Yusuf, 51. He is being held on $1 million bail, according to a criminal complaint filed in Hennepin County District Court.The incident occurred shortly before 1 am in Hopkins, a suburb of Minneapolis. Yusuf was on a phone call with his brother, who also works as an Uber driver, when he picked up Patel, court documents said.The brother allegedly heard the passenger tell Yusuf that he did not like his name, Mohamed, CBS News reported.As per the complaint, Patel used a seatbelt to strangle Yusuf before taking control of the vehicle. Yusuf was then run over and left in a ditch. Police believe the vehicle may have returned to the scene and struck him a second time.Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced the charges on Tuesday, describing the incident as an “incredibly brutal attack”.Yusuf sustained multiple serious injuries, including broken ribs, a fractured leg, spinal damage, collapsed lungs and extensive internal bleeding. The complaint states that several of his organs had to be removed.His family said he has undergone several operations and remains in a coma at Hennepin County Medical Centre in Minneapolis. His son, Mustafa Osman, said the family was struggling to deal with the extent of his father's injuries.Relatives believe the assault was driven by hatred, prompting calls from civil rights advocates for authorities to investigate it as a possible hate crime.However, Moriarty said prosecutors could not establish the required evidence to bring a bias-related charge. Under Minnesota law, authorities must demonstrate that a crime was deliberately motivated by prejudice against a protected characteristic.“We cannot criminally charge someone who may hold biased beliefs …. We must be able to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the criminal act was motivated by those biased beliefs,” Moriarty said, according to KSTP.She added that the decision not to pursue a hate crime charge did not lessen the suffering of Yusuf's family or the wider Somali community.Yusuf had worked as a taxi and ride-hailing driver for several years. His family described him as a dedicated father who was known for his empathy and ability to calm difficult situations.The attack has also raised concerns among Minnesota's Somali-American community, the largest Somali population in the United States, with many residents based in the Minneapolis-St Paul metropolitan area.You use AI every day. articles.summary: AHMEDABAD: The Gujarat Anti-Terrorist Squad (ATS) has busted an organised crude oil pilferage racket and arrested five individuals following a raid near

articles.title: House Republican pushes minerals, trade for peace in escalating Ethiopia, Eritrea crisis
articles.summary: A House Republican is looking to leverage U.S. food exports, agricultural equipment and know-how to coax Ethiopia and Eritrea towards peace, in dual legislation expected to be introduced Thursday and shared exclusively with The Hill. The move also aims to draw the countries away from ties with China. Rep. Jim Baird (R-Ind.) is behind the…
articles.body:
A House Republican is looking to leverage U.S. food exports, agricultural equipment and know-how to coax Ethiopia and Eritrea towards peace, in dual legislation expected to be introduced Thursday and shared exclusively with The Hill. The move also aims to draw the countries away from ties with China.

Rep. Jim Baird (R-Ind.) is behind the Ethiopia SPARK Act and Eritrea PILLAR Act. Both texts call for the countries to take steps toward establishing a lasting peace and then benefit from formal trade talks to increase exports of American agricultural products, equipment and know-how.

“African nations are primed for partnership,” Baird, a member of the House Foreign Affairs subcommittee on Africa, said in a statement to The Hill.

“The continent is rich in natural resources and home to a young, growing population eager for greater economic opportunity. In Indiana and across America’s heartland, we have the agricultural expertise and technological know-how to help unlock that potential and build lasting economic partnerships.”

Baird’s legislation aims to trade progress on peace for Ethiopia and Eritrean access to foodstuffs like corn, soybeans, soybean meal and livestock feed, farm equipment, and agricultural research and technical expertise. It also aims to put the U.S. as a preferred partner compared to China, which has deep ties in both countries.

“East Africa has tremendous potential, with the benefit of limited influence from America’s adversaries, like China,” Baird said.

The legislation also calls for U.S. assistance in mining some of the region’s critical minerals: gold, silver, copper, zinc, iron, ore, potash, cement and limestone, natural gas and oil, among others, as well as access to the country’s port infrastructures. The U.S. could leverage reduced tariffs and better trade terms.

“East Africa could seriously benefit from this economic opportunity, which can be a powerful foundation for lasting peace and prosperity,” Baird said in a statement.

“Our engagement also sends a broader message across the continent: African nations willing to pursue peaceful cooperation and economic growth will find a willing partner across the Atlantic.”

Baird’s legislation comes as Ethiopia and Eritrea appear poised for all-out war, adding greater instability to a region already wracked with conflict.

The Trump administration has also put forth diplomatic efforts. Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali on Oct. 14, discussing heightened tensions with Eritrea and called for a return to the 2018 Ethiopia-Eritrea peace framework.

“The Secretary stressed that all countries in the Horn of Africa must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors and avoid cross-border incursions. The Secretary emphasized that the region cannot tolerate more conflict.”

Troop buildups along the shared border have brought Ethiopian and Eritrean forces within striking distance of each other, Reuters reported on Wednesday. The buildup comes on top of an outbreak of fighting in September between the Ethiopian federal government and rebels in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.

Democrats focused on Africa have also raised concern about the risk of escalating conflict, writing to Rubio in a letter dated Nov. 10 urging “sustained and coordinated diplomatic engagement” to lower the temperature.

“The situation could lead to a multi-front conflict that would risk destabilizing Ethiopia the broader Horn of Africa, the Red Sea, our partners in the Gulf, and vital shipping lanes. The United States should bring new diplomatic energy and policy tools to bear before the conflict escalates further,” they wrote.

articles.title: UN top court finds Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against Rohingya minority
articles.summary: Myanmar committed genocide against the country’s long-persecuted Rohingya minority, the United Nations’ top court found Thursday, an unprecedented ruling that survivors of the atrocities have waited almost a decade to hear.
articles.body: Myanmar committed genocide against the country’s long-persecuted Rohingya minority, the United Nations’ top court found Thursday, an unprecedented ruling that survivors of the atrocities have waited almost a decade to hear. The historic judgement marks the first time the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also known as the World Court, has held a state accountable for genocide in its 80-year history — and the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar. The court’s decision — by nine votes to six — also comes at a time when the broader idea of international justice has come under fire from the Trump administration. For the Rohingya, the ICJ’s judgment is a “turning point.” “It is the difference between being told our history was a tragedy, and being told our history was a crime that must be answered for,” said Murshid Alam, who was just 12 years old when he was driven from his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state. The ICJ’s rulings are final and binding, but the court — which hears disputes between states — doesn’t have the power to enforce its decisions. Its orders, however, are sent to the UN Security Council, which could decide to implement the court’s ruling through a resolution. Between 2016 and 2017, the military in Buddhist-majority Myanmar targeted villages and towns home to Rohingya communities, looting, burning and slaughtering their inhabitants, and expelling hundreds of thousands from the country. CNN reporting at the time documented harrowing stories from Rohingya who saw their family members raped or killed by soldiers, and in some case their Buddhist neighbors joining in the massacres. Photos showed streams of terrified people fleeing burning villages on foot or piling into overcrowded boats as they sought to reach neighboring Bangladesh and safety. This case against Myanmar was brought in 2019 by The Gambia, a country thousands of miles from where the killings took place, in a world-first. The United States and Canada previously declared the atrocities as genocide. After seven years of weighing evidence and hearing witness testimony, the ICJ found that the scale and nature of Myanmar’s atrocities were “characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group,” presiding judge Iwasawa Yuji said during a nearly three-hour reading. “The court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy” the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state. In its judgment, the court established the military “engaged in indiscriminate killings” and gave particular weight to the “widespread acts of sexual violence, and extreme acts of violence against children” as well as security forces’ attacks on “Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh.” Myanmar had denied its “clearance operations” were intended to destroy the Rohingya population, and said the military was conducting legitimate counterterrorism operations against a Rohingya insurgent group. The court rejected that defense, saying the Myanmar military did not distinguish between militants and civilians. CNN has reached out to Myanmar’s military-backed government for comment on the ruling. ‘The world sees our suffering’ Murshid Alam was a child when he was forced out of his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state by a hail of gunfire. In the chaos of the escape, he was shot in his ear — a “terrifying experience,” he told CNN. The wound has healed, but the “secondary trauma of losing my home and seeing my community destroyed” has not. Alam was one of more than 740,000 Rohingya people who fled to Bangladesh to escape the massacres. The sprawling refugee camps that he came of age in have since become the world’s largest, hosting more than 1.2 million people. “Our generation has grown up in displacement. We have known nothing but statelessness,” said Alam, 22, who now works to educate and advocate for young people in the Cox’s Bazar camps as founder of the Rohingya Youth Union. The genocide ruling, he said, “tells us that the world sees our suffering and refuses to let it be erased.” UN human rights chief Volker Türk told CNN the judgment was “historic” and particularly striking for the way it examined “the decades of discrimination and marginalization of the Rohingya.” Following The Gambia’s successful application to bring the case, the ICJ allowed South Africa to bring a case against Israel over its war with Hamas in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. Israel denies the genocide charge. That has led to concerns among some the court could come into collision with the Trump administration – already on a campaign to “dismantle” another institution, the International Criminal Court. Last month, its UN ambassador Mike Waltz accused the ICJ of trying to lower the threshold for a genocide verdict in the Myanmar case that he claimed could potentially be “weaponized” against American soldiers. A US State Department spokesperson told CNN in a statement Thursday they “are studying the decision to fully assess its implications.” “The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ,” the spokesperson added. What next for the Rohingya? The ICJ ordered Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingya, including to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return to their place of residence and reunification of families,” and return all property lost or damaged. It also ordered Myanmar to ensure their future protection from discrimination and persecution. It is unlikely Myanmar will adhere. The head of the Myanmar military during the massacres, Min Aung Hlaing is now the country’s leader after he overthrew the elected government – and has dismissed the Rohingya identity as “imaginary.” His military-backed government has shown little interest in allowing Rohingya to return. What they would return to is another question. In the Rohingya homeland of Rakhine state, the military-backed government is not in control. An ethnic armed group called the Arakan Army controls the vast majority of the state, including areas that border Bangladesh, and has been accused of widespread abuses against civilians in its areas. Meanwhile, the military has ramped up airstrikes across the state as part of its grinding civil war, dropping bombs on civilian markets and hospitals, in response to territorial losses. Rohingya now living in the camps cannot work and face dire conditions, including trafficking, exploitation, meagre food rations, and a lack of basic education. Alam, in the Bangladesh refugee camp, hoped the ruling could pave the way for a return to the home he fled as a young boy. “The Rohingya do not want to live in refugee camps forever. We want to return to our homeland in Rakhine state with our rights, our citizenship, and our dignity fully restored,” he said.

articles.title: Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift performs with Keith Urban
articles.summary: Langley won six awards, weeks after her hit Choosin' Texas broke a Billboard chart record in the US.
articles.body:
US singer Ella Langley has swept the Country Music Association Awards (CMAs), following the huge success of her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas.

The Alabama-born singer was named entertainer of the year at Wednesday's ceremony, weeks after the song became the longest-running number one in Billboard chart history.

"At this point, I'm sick of me," the 27-year-old joked in her acceptance speech, having spent so much of the ceremony on stage. "I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life."

Choosin' Texas was also named single of the year and song of the year, leading Langley to joke in an acceptance speech: "This song is the gift that keeps on giving."

Langley won six awards in total, including female vocalist of the year, music video of the year and album of the year for Dandelion.

She also performed her song Loving Life Again with a string quartet, and duetted with Miranda Lambert for a performance of Snakeskin Boots.

Choosin' Texas made history in September after spending 23 weeks at the top spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. It has now spent 28 weeks in total at the summit.

Following her win, Langley took to social media and said: "Hard to put this night into words and what it means.

"Thank you to my fans. Thank you for loving this record, thank you for coming to my shows, thank you for believing in my artistry.

"This year has been the most incredible journey, and I want to thank you for sharing in that with me. I love y'all."

Taylor Swift also performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years.

Her performance began with Swift walking backstage and featured cameo appearances from country stars including Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Sugarland, and Brooks & Dunn.

Swift then sang her recent hit I Knew It, I Knew You, from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack, using a blue guitar with bedazzled clouds on it, in a nod to the animated franchise.

The singer also mixed in some of her 2006 country hit Our Song, while Keith Urban joined her on the banjo.

Swift's performance came after she was inducted into both the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame earlier this year.

Other winners on the night included Chris Stapleton who won male vocalist of the year, The Red Clay Strays who won vocal group of the year, and Brooks & Dunn with vocal duo of the year.

Meanwhile Stephen Wilson Jr won the new artist of the year award while Charlie Worsham won musician of the year.

The award ceremony began with a tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, who died in August aged 80.

Ceremony host Lainey Wilson began the tribute by duetting with singer-songwriter Vince Gill on a rendition of Parton's I Will Always Love You.

articles.title: Trump, Xi, Putin issue 4-point ‘declaration toward peace’ after summit
articles.summary: President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a four-point “peace declaration” following their unprecedented summit in China on Thursday. The world leaders addressed United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court and nuclear conflict, according to text released by all three countries. The declaration states that as permanent…
articles.body:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a four-point “peace declaration” following their unprecedented summit in China on Thursday.

The world leaders addressed United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court and nuclear conflict, according to text released by all three countries.

The declaration states that as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, all three countries are “committed to promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges” and intend to plan to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”

They also agreed “that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction” and reaffirmed that a nuclear war must never be fought

“The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons,” it reads.

Trump met Putin and Xi in Shenzhen, China, early Thursday for a historic 90-minute trilateral meeting.

“We have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful, and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people but the entire planet,” Trump said in opening remarks, before the meeting was closed to the press.

“Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite,” he continued. “I think that we are sure about that. No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about it. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.”

The president indicated in the lead-up to the summit that he would like to discuss the Iran conflict, the Russia-Ukraine war and denuclearization.

Washington has backed Ukraine in its effort to prevent Russia from taking over the country, while China has helped support Russia. Meanwhile, Iran has also received some aid from Moscow and Beijing in its war with the U.S.

On nuclear nonproliferation, China has resisted checks on its buildup of nuclear weapons.

However, during Thursday’s bilateral meeting, Xi said, “Nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world,” according to China’s Xinhua News Agency.

articles.body:
China blocked a Bloomberg reporter from being in the room to cover the opening remarks of President Trump’s trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

According to the White House press pool report, the Bloomberg reporter was blocked from the event because she asked a question during Trump’s bilateral with Xi earlier in the day.

“A Bloomberg reporter was barred from this spray because she asked a question during the bilateral meeting with Xi,” the pool report read. “A WH [White House] official said they pushed to have her reinstated but Chinese officials insisted she be excluded.”

Bloomberg reporter Annmarie Hordern had asked Trump during his bilateral with Xi if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been disloyal to the U.S. Trump did not respond to the question.

The move to shut out a journalist from covering a meeting is an example of China’s restrictions on press access. It is not unusual in the U.S. for reporters to shout questions at the president and foreign leaders during on-camera meetings and events.

Trump appeared to criticize other press restrictions during the trip earlier on Thursday.

“It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it, because every move was perfectly executed,” Trump said, referring to the summit.

The three leaders addressed United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court and nuclear conflict, according to text released by Russia and China.

articles.title: Trump greets Putin: ‘He’s my friend’
articles.summary: President Trump greeted Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “friend” Thursday, as the two arrived for a meeting in China. “Who is he? He’s my friend.” Trump is heard saying, after walking into a room with his Russian counterpart. Trump, who has long had a friendly relationship with Putin, was set to speak separately with…
articles.body:
President Trump greeted Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “friend” Thursday, as the two arrived for a meeting in China.

“Who is he? He’s my friend.” Trump is heard saying , after walking into a room with his Russian counterpart.

Trump, who has long had a friendly relationship with Putin, was set to speak separately with the leader during a trip to Shenzhen, China, aside from the planned trilateral with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The talks mark their first one-on-one since an Alaska summit in August 2025, which was meant to further negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

Earlier this week, Trump told reporters he believed the Russian president was “backing down a bit” in the war in Ukraine, which will hit the five-year mark in February.

“I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” the president said. “I think he’s backing down. I think he’d like to, frankly, I think he’d like to see it finished.”

During the trilateral meeting Thursday, the three superpowers established a “declaration toward peace.”

Back in the U.S., Republican lawmakers had mixed reactions to Trump’s coziness toward Xi and Putin.

Some have said they thought the meeting between the three leaders was a bad indication of U.S. priorities. Others said they supported an American leader who was open to having intense discussions with powerful countries.

“I’ve never been successful in getting inside the president’s head, but I can tell you where I am, we have to be more clear about who our friends are and who our allies are,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said.

articles.title: A geography of hearts: Turkiye and Lebanon, building the Levant together
articles.summary: Turkiye and Lebanon can build a stronger Levant through partnership, sovereignty and mutual respect.
articles.body:
Some journeys feel less like a first visit and more like a homecoming. That is how I felt during my three days in Lebanon — my first ever visit to a country I had long known through its history, its poets and its people, but had never walked through myself.

I came at the kind invitation of Dr Tarek Mitri, Deputy Prime Minister of Lebanon, who proved the most gracious of hosts. I came in a spirit of friendship and partnership, and I leave with gratitude. In every conversation — in Beirut, in Tripoli, in Akkar and beyond — I heard the same quiet determination: Lebanon wants to stand on its own feet, and it wants partners, not patrons.

I also leave with a full heart and, I must admit, a fuller stomach. From a za’atar breakfast on the road to Akkar to the sweets of Hallab in Tripoli and shawarma at Barbar in Beirut, Lebanese hospitality is everything people promise. Around shared tables, over strong coffee and long conversations, I was reminded that the bonds between our peoples were never only about diplomacy. Distance on a map tells you very little. What matters is the geography of hearts — and by that measure, Beirut and Istanbul have always been neighbours.

That warmth carries a responsibility, for friendship is proved not in words but in what we do together. Five convictions stayed with me throughout the visit.

Lebanon’s diversity of faiths, communities and traditions is not a weakness to be managed; it is a richness to be protected. I was honoured to meet leaders from across the country’s political and spiritual life: President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and the veteran Speaker of Parliament, Nabih Berri; the Grand Mufti of the Lebanese Republic, Sheikh Abdul Latif Derian, and the Greek Orthodox Metropolitan of Beirut, His Eminence Elias Audi; Mrs Bahia Hariri, Vice President of the Future Movement; and Mr Walid Jumblatt, former leader of the Progressive Socialist Party. Different as their paths have been, each spoke of the same hope: a state that serves all its citizens, institutions that work and a future their children will not have to leave the country to find. National unity is the foundation on which everything else — security, recovery, prosperity — must be built. Turkiye’s interest is in a strong, whole and united Lebanon.

2. Lebanon’s decisions belong to the Lebanese

For too long, Lebanon has paid the price of being treated as an arena for the rivalries of others. That has to end. Nowhere is this felt more deeply than in the south, whose towns, farmland and families have borne the heaviest cost of this year’s war. Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity are not negotiable — and they must extend to every inch of its land. Occupation in the south must end, and the Lebanese state must be able to protect all of its citizens, from Beirut to the southern border. The choices about Lebanon’s future must be made in Beirut, by Lebanese, for Lebanese. Foreign states — near or far — should respect that. Real friends offer support when it is asked for and step back when it is not. That is the principle Turkiye seeks to live by.

3. A Levant-driven future, built on trade

The problems of our region will not be solved one capital at a time, and they will not be solved from outside. The Levant must think and act as a region, as it once did. The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus records that the Phoenician cities held their common council in Tripoli, gathering there to deliberate on matters of the greatest importance. More than 2,000 years later, our region urgently needs to recover that tradition of meeting, talking and deciding together, and Tripoli, which welcomed me so warmly, is a fitting place to begin. Our economies are natural complements: Lebanon’s entrepreneurial talent, its banking and services heritage and its ports; Turkiye’s manufacturing base, logistics networks and access to Europe and Central Asia. As Syria recovers, a corridor of trade, transport and energy linking our countries can become the backbone of a new regional economy. Let goods, investment and young people’s ideas move freely across our region, and stability will follow prosperity.

Turkiye does not come to Lebanon with new slogans; we come with a track record. We have stood behind UNIFIL’s peacekeeping mission in the south. Through TİKA and the Turkish Red Crescent, we have delivered humanitarian aid in Lebanon’s hardest hours. Now the task is to rebuild the south — its homes and schools, its hospitals and roads and its olive groves — so that every displaced family can return home with dignity. Turkiye stands ready to play its full part in that effort, and to help strengthen the Lebanese institutions that must lead it. We have consistently defended Lebanon’s sovereignty in every international forum, and we will continue to do so. Through the foundations and educational institutions I work with, we have seen firsthand how much Lebanese students and young people have to offer — and how much our two societies gain when they learn side by side.

In a fragile world, no country prospers alone. Cooperation between Turkiye and Lebanon is not charity flowing in one direction; it is interdependence that strengthens both. When Lebanon is stable, Turkiye and the whole region are safer. When Lebanese businesses grow, Turkish businesses gain partners. When our universities, civil society and young people connect, both nations gain. The goal is a partnership of equals — one where each side brings its strengths and neither loses its independence.

I leave Lebanon convinced that the moment for deeper partnership is now. Lebanon has endured more than its share of war, economic hardship and loss — especially this year, and the south most of all. Yet what I saw was not a country defeated but a people ready to rebuild. Turkiye will be there — not as a distant benefactor, but as a neighbour in the geography of hearts — until the last family has returned to its village in the south and the last school has reopened its doors. I hope this was the first of many visits, and that the friendships begun over these three days grow into lasting partnerships between our institutions, our businesses and, above all, our young people.

Shukran, Lebanon. Tesekkurler. Until we meet again.

articles.title: Fake epilepsy, diabetes drugs made using chalk, lactose at illegal Himachal factory; 2 held
articles.summary: MEERUT/SHIMLA: An illegal pharmaceutical factory allegedly manufacturing counterfeit medicines used to treat epilepsy, diabetes, typhoid and other
articles.body: MEERUT/SHIMLA: An illegal pharmaceutical factory allegedly manufacturing counterfeit medicines used to treat epilepsy, diabetes, typhoid and other ailments using substances such as chalk and lactose was busted in Himachal Pradesh's Solan district on Thursday following a joint operation by Uttar Pradesh Special Task Force (STF) and drug authorities. Two men were arrested from the unit, which operated without a manufacturing licence from a residential building in Rajpura village near Nalagarh. Investigators recovered nearly 67,000 antibiotic tablets, 6,500 Pregabalin capsules, raw materials and machinery used to manufacture and package the drugs.The raid followed an investigation into counterfeit medicines seized from a medical shop in Kuraina village of Varanasi on Oct 30. Pharmaceutical companies whose brand names appeared on the seized medicines identified them as spurious, prompting police to register an FIR. On Wednesday, UP STF and Varanasi police arrested Abhishek Singh for allegedly distributing counterfeit medicines in Bihar and Jharkhand. During questioning, he disclosed that the drugs were being sourced from the Solan factory, leading investigators to the unit.The factory allegedly manufactured Pregabalin capsules (used to treat epilepsy, seizures and neuropathic pain); C-Z tablets containing Cefixime and Azithromycin (prescribed for bacterial infections, including typhoid and urinary tract infections); PAN D (used to treat acid reflux and ulcers); and Metformin Hydrochloride (prescribed for type 2 diabetes). Investigators also recovered raw drug pellets and packaging materials. Pregabalin falls under Schedule H1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, while the other prescription medicines are regulated under Schedule H. These medicines require prescriptions from registered medical practitioners.Additional SP Brijesh Kumar Singh of UP STF's Meerut field unit said the accused were using chalk and lactose as raw materials to manufacture counterfeit medicines. "We've arrested two men from the factory. Raw materials used to make these drugs were chalk and lactose," Singh said.The arrested men, Monu Mehta from Jharkhand and Mohammad Haseen from Saharanpur, operated the manufacturing machinery and handled dispatches. Singh said they were recruited by Sunil Kumar, a Badaun resident who allegedly owned the factory and had previously been arrested and jailed in a counterfeit medicine case in Varanasi. Sunil remained absconding. The two men received monthly salaries of Rs 15,000 to Rs 20,000. Haseen had joined the unit seven months earlier, while Mehta had worked there for about a year.A joint team of Meerut UP STF, UP Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) and Himachal Pradesh State Drugs Control Administration raided the premises. Himachal Pradesh state drug controller Manish Kapoor told TOI that his department received information from UP STF and FSDA on Wednesday evening and immediately formed a team of five drug inspectors. "We constituted a team of five drug inspectors, carried out search and seizure operation entire night and arrested two persons with nearly 67,000 antibiotic tablets and 6,500 Pregabalin capsules," Kapoor said.The search also yielded two capsule-filling machines, blister-packing machines, an air compressor, unfinished pharmaceutical materials and packaging equipment. Investigators found that the unit lacked a manufacturing licence and that the seized medicines carried labels falsely claiming they were manufactured in Sirmaur district of Himachal Pradesh. Kapoor said the products were suspected to be substandard and authorities were examining the manufacturing and distribution network.Dr Harish Mohan Rastogi, a physician, warned that counterfeit medicines could put patients at serious risk, particularly those undergoing treatment for epilepsy, diabetes and infections. "Some of these are lifesaving drugs like Pregabalin and Metformin Hydrochloride meant to treat kidney infections, epilepsy and diabetes. The counterfeit one will not affect the patients, leading to emergencies and can be life-threatening. Similarly, others are antibiotics for different infections like typhoid and allergies," he told TOI.The FIR registered in Varanasi invoked BNS sections 61(2) (criminal conspiracy), 111 (organised crime), 318(4) (cheating involving delivery of property), 336(3) (forgery with intent to cheat), 276 (adulteration of drugs) and 278 (selling a drug as a different drug). A Nalagarh court remanded Mehta and Haseen to the custody of Himachal Pradesh State Drugs Control Administration until Nov 23. articles.body: Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday blamed his predecessor Sheikh Hasina and her party for the fresh spell of arson attacks in the country.Ahead of Hasina's proposed return in December, Rahman said that people no longer wanted politics involving arson, enforced disappearances and killings, The Daily Star reported.“Enough is enough. articles.title: The road to victory in Iran goes through Kyiv
articles.summary: The most promising road to victory in Iran does not run through another round of bombing Tehran. It runs through the defeat of Putin’s Russia.
articles.body:
Vice President JD Vance blamed the Republican midterm defeat primarily on the war with Iran. But perhaps the problem was not the war itself. It was the absence of a clearly defined goal, a questionable strategy and the failure to achieve victory.

After months of American and Israeli bombardment, Iran’s military and economy have suffered enormous damage. Yet its regime has not capitulated. We have failed to eliminate or even weaken it. Destroying military capabilities does not necessarily destroy a totalitarian regime. As long as it controls its population, it can replace leaders and divert disproportionate resources toward continued aggression.

The Soviet Union illustrates the paradox. It emerged from World War II having lost approximately 27 million people , with its economy devastated. Yet Stalin’s regime had never been stronger. It consolidated power at home and imposed Communist rule across Eastern Europe . The country was exhausted; the regime was triumphant.

Iran may be experiencing a similar dynamic. Foreign attacks can help its rulers mobilize nationalism, tighten ideological control and denounce opponents as traitors. We cannot expect a different outcome merely by continuing to bomb. We need to review our strategy.

Two fundamental mistakes lie at the heart of our approach: a poor understanding of the nature of totalitarian regimes and a failure to recognize the ideological character of the aggressive wars they wage. The first mistake leads to the false assumption that destroying a country’s military capabilities, and economy will necessarily weaken its regime and bring it closer to capitulation. But unless military force destroys the regime completely, it may actually strengthen it.

And to destroy and replace the regime completely can be an extraordinarily costly undertaking. Nazi Germany’s defeat required unconditional surrender, occupation, the dismantling of Nazi institutions and the establishment of a democratic order. Such an undertaking in Iran would demand sacrifices Americans are unlikely to accept.

Our second mistake is failing to recognize the nature of the war. The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine are not separate regional struggles. They are interconnected fronts in a global ideological war between the democratic world and a united bloc of totalitarian states: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

This bloc is bound together by mutual support agreements and concrete cooperation. Iran has supplied drones to Russia, North Korea has provided weapons and troops and China supplies crucial industrial and technological inputs. We cannot split it through separate deals that appease some of its members. Our attempts to accommodate Putin’s regime have not stopped it from providing Iran with intelligence, and military assistance used against our troops and allies in the Middle East.

Treating these adversaries separately overlooks how gains by one can strengthen the others. A Russian victory in Ukraine would embolden its partners and weaken American deterrence. A Ukrainian victory could have the opposite effect on Tehran and strengthen the American position in the region.

These realities demand a consistent American strategy. We cannot simultaneously confront one totalitarian dictatorship while accommodating and strengthening another. Eliminate Iranian ayatollahs while embracing Putin, Xi Jinping and Kim Jong Un.

Consider nuclear weapons. Trump said that Iran’s nuclear program was obliterated . Perhaps. But as long as Putin’s regime exists, the possibility of Russia transferring nuclear weapons to Iran cannot be entirely dismissed. By supporting Russia, we inevitably strengthen Iran. We need a consistent policy toward the entire totalitarian bloc. This does not require war with every member. It requires a consistent political and economic strategy — and the wisdom to concentrate our resources on its weakest link.

Russia’s economy remains heavily dependent on natural resources . Russia’s military, once considered overwhelmingly powerful, failed to seize Kyiv, surrendered a large part of the territories it had occupied and has faced Ukrainian resistance at enormous cost.

With sufficient Western assistance, Ukraine could counter Russian aggression. Stronger sanctions could simultaneously weaken Putin’s ability to sustain the war. Together, these pressures could create conditions for his regime’s collapse. That would weaken Iran materially by depriving it of a major ally.

But the ideological consequences might be even more important. The collapse of Soviet communism demoralized and brought an end to many totalitarian, and even authoritarian, regimes. So, the collapse of Putin’s totalitarianism, very similar to Iran’s, could demonstrate the vulnerability of this political model, discourage Iran’s rulers and encourage its opposition.

First, seek a temporary truce in Iran while maintaining economic and political pressure. A ceasefire need not confer legitimacy on the regime or amount to a permanent settlement.

Second, concentrate military assistance on Ukraine and intensify sanctions against Russia. A Russian defeat would reshape the strategic balance across the entire bloc.

Third, once Iran is weakened by the loss of its ally, pursue a peaceful offensive reminiscent of Ronald Reagan’s approach to Soviet communism: economic pressure, public diplomacy, ideological confrontation and support for dissidents and democratic opposition.

The most promising road to victory in Iran does not run through another round of bombing Tehran. It runs through the defeat of Putin’s Russia.

The road to victory in Iran goes through Kyiv.

Yuri Yarim-Agaev is president of the Center for the Study of Totalitarian Ideology and a member of the Moscow Helsinki Group .

articles.title: Danish Parliament approves US- Greenland security deal after Trump pressure
articles.summary: The Danish Parliament approved the U.S.-Greenland security deal this week, after pressure from President Trump to acquire the Arctic territory. The agreement, which Trump announced in September, will replace a previous deal signed between the U.S. and Denmark in 1951. It was approved by both the Danish and Greenlandic legislatures, according to a press release.…
articles.body:
The Danish Parliament approved the U.S.-Greenland security deal this week, after pressure from President Trump to acquire the Arctic territory.

The agreement, which Trump announced in September , will replace a previous deal signed between the U.S. and Denmark in 1951 . It was approved by both the Danish and Greenlandic legislatures, according to a press release.

When unveiling the plan, the president touted that Washington would have more say in Greenland’s business dealings and said the deal would allow for a larger U.S. military presence on the island, which would include two new bases .

He said in late September that the deal “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns.”

“Additionally, from now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post at the time.

In October, he also announced that “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration was set to begin in Greenland. But few details were given.

The Trump administration has repeatedly pushed Denmark and Greenland to allow the U.S. to take over the territory.

The rhetoric angered officials in both regions as well as NATO allies. The president and members of his Cabinet have cited national security as the reason for the pressure — sounding alarms over the possibility of China or Russia trying to conquer it.

“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many,” Trump wrote in September. “We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction.”

articles.title: White House officials seize reporter’s phones aboard Air Force One after China departure
articles.summary: White House officials unexpectedly seized mobile phones from journalists aboard Air Force One after leaving China, citing security reasons amidst high-level discussions with Chinese and Russian leaders.
articles.body: White House officials collected the mobile phones of journalists travelling with US President Donald Trump aboard Air Force One shortly after the aircraft departed China on Thursday, citing security concerns. The unexpected move left reporters without their devices as the presidential plane began its journey from Shenzhen.A pool reporter disclosed the development in a dispatch shortly after Trump boarded the aircraft at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport, saying journalists had been informed that their phones would be taken temporarily for security reasons. The reporters were not notified beforehand and learned about the arrangement only after taking their seats.NBC News correspondent Garrett Haake described the move as “unusual” in a post on X. Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich also raised questions about the aircraft's destination, suggesting that the collection of phones raised suspicion that Air Force One “may not be heading straight home”. The plane's intended destination remained unclear at the time of the report.The incident followed Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen. The trilateral discussions covered nuclear arms control and the US war with Iran.Trump had also indicated before leaving Washington that he could meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his Asia visit. Speaking to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, he said such a meeting could take place in China, but that the decision would rest with Xi. However, no meeting between Trump and Kim took place during the visit.North Korea's absence from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum and Kim's lack of participation in previous summits had raised doubts about his possible appearance in Shenzhen. South Korea's foreign minister had also expressed little expectation that the North Korean leader would attend.The collection of phones came after other security precautions during Trump's China visit. White House staff reportedly discarded Chinese-issued credentials, delegation pins and temporary phones near the aircraft stairs before departure, amid concerns that the devices could have been compromised.Journalists also faced restrictions during the president's engagements with foreign leaders. NBC News reported that Russian officials prevented two reporters from attending Trump's informal meeting with Putin. Chinese officials also excluded a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral meeting after the journalist shouted a question about Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.You use AI every day. articles.title: The GLP-1 blind spot: Why the FDA’s new eye stroke warning matters
articles.summary: It forces the medical community to treat these therapies with clinical gravity instead of casual enthusiasm.
articles.body:
The Food and Drug Administration’s drug safety communication on GLP-1 drugs should serve as a wake-up call for patient safety and corporate accountability.

The federal agency is forcing drugmakers to update warnings for blockbusters like Ozempic and Zepbound. They must now clearly state the risk of a rare, permanent blinding condition called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. This happens when sudden blocked blood flow to the optic nerve causes painless, irreversible vision loss. Right now, we have no medical treatment to reverse the damage.

The FDA stepped in after reviewing clinical trials, post-marketing data and adverse event reports, finding documented cases across all marketed GLP-1 drugs. This moves the U.S. into alignment with health regulators in Europe, the United Kingdom, Japan and Australia, which already require these safety updates.

From a statistical standpoint, the risk looks incredibly small. The FDA analyzed clinical trial data from over 134,000 patients. They found about 6.4 cases of this blinding condition per 100,000 for those on GLP-1 drugs, compared to 3.8 cases in the control group.

Drug advocates are quick to point out that a difference of fewer than 3 cases per 100,000 people is practically microscopic next to the massive metabolic and weight loss benefits of these therapies. But as a physician leader, I have to look at the scale. An estimated 45 to 48 million Americans have used these medications. Multiply a tiny statistical variation across a population that large, and we are suddenly talking about thousands of real people facing permanent blindness.

The tipping point for federal scientists was a landmark study published in JAMA Ophthalmology that originally flagged this heightened risk profile.

This mandate lands right in the middle of a major legal crisis for the pharmaceutical industry. Dozens of personal injury lawsuits filed by patients who suffered permanent eye damage have been combined into a federal mass tort case in Pennsylvania. The plaintiffs allege that manufacturers saw early signals of vascular eye damage but left them off the product labels, depriving patients of genuine, informed consent. Drugmakers are fighting back aggressively.

Novo Nordisk points out that current observational data cannot prove direct biological causation. Their lawyers argue that the exact conditions driving people to take GLP-1s — for example, Type 2 diabetes, severe obesity and high blood pressure — are already independent, well-documented risk factors for eye diseases.

For the last few years, the cultural conversation around GLP-1s has been incredibly commercialized. It has been reduced to celebrity lifestyle trends and digital health ads. This casual framing has completely masked a hard truth: These are potent, systemic medications that impact multiple organ systems.

The FDA’s class-wide mandate is a necessary policy correction. It forces the medical community to treat these therapies with clinical gravity instead of casual enthusiasm. True medical progress can never be measured just by market adoption or quarterly revenue. It must be measured by complete transparency and the safety of our patients.

Eric Wargotz is a physician, judge and professor, and the 178th president of MedChi, the Maryland State Medical Society .

articles.title: 5 takeaways on Trump’s unprecedented summit with Putin, Xi
articles.summary: President Trump wrapped a whirlwind three-day trip to Asia on Thursday with an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The president struck trade deals with the Philippines and Thailand during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila earlier in the week. But the highest-profile stop…
articles.body:
President Trump wrapped a whirlwind three-day trip to Asia on Thursday with an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The president struck trade deals with the Philippines and Thailand during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila earlier in the week.

But the highest-profile stop on Trump’s Asia tour was in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Xi and Putin both one-on-one and then together.

Democrats hammered Trump for the public coziness with America’s rivals, but the president argued the “old school” of diplomacy hasn’t been working.

Here are five takeaways from Trump’s trip to Asia.

US, Russia, China agree to dialogue on nuclear nonproliferation

As part of a four-point “declaration toward peace” released after Thursday’s summit, Trump, Putin and Xi agreed to participate in an ongoing dialogue on nuclear nonproliferation.

“The three heads of state reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons,” the three leaders said in the joint statement.

The U.S., China and Russia are the world’s largest nuclear powers.

“It’s not an easy thing to do, give them up,” Trump said of nuclear arms, seated across from Putin and Xi. “But it’s also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That’s what we’re doing in Iran.”

Observers and U.S. officials had low expectations that any major breakthroughs would be reached with China because of the country’s past resistance to checks on nuclear arms buildup.

“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior U.S. official told reporters last week, referring to the meeting as “an entry point.”

China is a member of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, but the Pentagon has estimated the country will likely have more than 1,000 operational nuclear warheads by 2030.

Shots fired at International Criminal Court

The three countries used the joint declaration to levy criticism against the International Criminal Court (ICC), calling on the body to not “abuse” its jurisdiction.

“The three heads of state recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction,” the leaders said in the declaration.

In 2023, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Putin over alleged war crimes related to the deportation of Ukrainian children as a part of Russia’s war in Ukraine.

The Trump administration has been an outspoken opponent of the ICC, largely over its prosecution of Israeli leaders over alleged war crimes in Gaza.

Earlier this year, Secretary of State Marco Rubio pledged that the U.S. would dismantle the international body “brick by brick.”

While Russia voted in favor of the Rome Statute establishing the court in 1998, China and the U.S. voted against it.

Trump cozies up to Putin as Ukraine war rages on

Trump discussed Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine with Putin and Xi during their meetings Thursday, saying that his Russian counterpart would like to see the war ended.

“We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have.

“President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while, that’s what pretty, pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening,” Trump said during his trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.

Trump went on to refer to Ukraine as “the other side” in his remarks.

“I think that he [Putin], and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war,” Trump said.

Trump was outwardly warm toward Putin during their meetings, referring to his Russian counterpart as “his friend” in their first meeting since their summit in Alaska last year.

“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said walking into the room to greet Putin on Thursday.

Russia’s war in Ukraine is in its fifth year, but that was not mentioned in the joint declaration between the three countries.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday that Xi and Trump could pressure Putin into ending the war.

“If China and the United States will put sanctions, or will say that they will put sanctions, stop export-import trade between Russia and these countries, that’s the end of the war,” Zelensky said in an interview with NBC News.

Trump reaches trade agreements with Philippines, Thailand

Prior to traveling to China, Trump announced two separate trade agreements with Thailand and the Philippines during the ASEAN summit in Manila.

Trump touted what he said was a “landmark” deal with the Philippines on Wednesday, saying it would be great for farmers and those in the energy business.

Trump praised the deal during a state lunch with the country’s president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

“It’s a fair deal for both countries, and we’re very happy with that, and we didn’t know that that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly,” Trump said.

On Tuesday, Trump announced that as part of a trade deal with the U.S., Thailand would slash all tariffs on U.S. exports and remove substantial nontariff barriers on various products.

Trump also noted that Thailand will purchase $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products, and the deal will be finalized in the coming weeks.

“We’ve been working on this deal for a long time,” the president said.

In a Truth Social post Thursday, the president said he would discuss both trade deals — and the rest of the trip — during a news conference Friday at the White House.

Trump did not hold a press conference in Asia, as is typical of U.S. presidents at the end of high-profile trips abroad.

He did give an interview to NBC News’s Gabe Gutierrez on the flight back home.

“I think it was a 12. On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12. It went great, “ Trump said of the trip. “Fantastic relationships built.”

He also said he and Xi talked about artificial intelligence guardrails during their meeting.

Media coverage of the summit was tightly controlled.

China barred a Bloomberg reporter from covering the trilateral meeting between the three leaders after the reporter shouted a question during Xi’s bilateral with Trump.

Bloomberg reporter Annmarie Hordern had asked Trump during his bilateral with Xi if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been disloyal to the U.S. Trump did not respond to the question.

Trump lightly criticized other press restrictions during the trip earlier Thursday.

“It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it, because every move was perfectly executed,” Trump said, referring to the summit.

articles.title: Star Wars actor Osian Morgan 'thrilled' to voice the Welsh Luke Skywalker
articles.summary: The classic 1977 film has been dubbed into Welsh for the first time and features a host of star names.
articles.body:
Voicing Luke Skywalker in the Welsh-language version of Star Wars was a "dream job" according to actor Osian Morgan.

The Cardiff-born actor said he loved the film series as a child and playing one of the lead roles was "very exciting".

Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd - based on the original 1977 film Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope - was given its first showing at a red-carpet event in Cardiff on Thursday.

The dubbed Welsh version, featuring actors Matthew Rhys and Rhys Ifans, will be broadcast publicly for the first time by S4C on Christmas Day.

Almost half a century since A New Hope was first released, the sci-fi universe created by George Lucas remains one of the biggest film franchises of all time.

It has been translated into over 50 languages, with Welsh becoming its most recent.

"It feels very exciting, it's thrilling," said Morgan, who has previously starred in Welsh language soap opera Pobol y Cwm and in BBC drama Waterloo Road.

His family attended the first screening of Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd, and Morgan admitted his youngest brother had never seen any of the films before.

"Shout out to him because the first time he gets to see it in Welsh is great," he said.

Mark Lewis Jones, who voices the dark lord Darth Vader, said on the red carpet it was "nice to record the voice but not have the make-up" and joked that "the Rhosllanerchrugog accent lends itself to the dark side".

Llyr Ifans, who plays C-3PO, said he hoped the film was successful and that more Welsh-language versions would follow.

"C-3PO seems to be in all of them," he said.

"I'm quite confident it will go down well and there will be a lot of happy Welsh-speaking parents on Christmas Day."

Ifans said he been a fan of the Star Wars films since childhood, and getting invited to play the character was "surreal".

"When I first got the email through I thought 'wow, this is a bit weird doing Star Wars in Welsh' but playing C-3PO, one of the iconic parts, you can't say no, can you really?"

C-3PO is said to be fluent in six million forms of communication and Ifans said it was now one more.

Prominent actors have lent their voices to the film's most famous characters, including Matthew Rhys (Han Solo), Rhys Ifans (Obi-Wan Kenobi) and Aimee-Ffion Edwards (Princess Leia).

Other voice actors in the Welsh version include Nia Roberts, Ioan Hefin, Richard Harrington, Owain Arthur, Rhodri Meilir, Richard Elfyn and Steffan Donnelly. The film is directed by Ellyn Stern.

The Welsh-language version was announced at the National Eisteddfod in Pembrokeshire in August, with Lucasfilm co-president Lynwen Brennan saying the franchise was keen to expand its horizons.

"As someone who was born and raised in Wales, seeing the audience reaction to iconic Star Wars moments retold in the Welsh language was a moment of great pride," she said.

S4C chief executive Geraint Evans added that working with "one of the most iconic and influential film franchises of all time is a tremendous honour".

"It is a unique opportunity to introduce the Welsh language to new audiences around the world, while showcasing Wales and its exceptional creative talent on a global stage," he said.

articles.title: UN court rules that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.summary: The United Nations’s International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found in a new ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim population, following thousands of deaths amid the county’s “clearance operations” in 2017. The Hague-based world court said Myanmar violated its obligation to prevent the destruction of evidence in connection with allegations of…
articles.body:
The United Nations’s International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found in a new ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim population , following thousands of deaths amid the county’s “clearance operations” in 2017.

The Hague-based world court said Myanmar violated its obligation to prevent the destruction of evidence in connection with allegations of genocide, and that it violated obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention to punish those who committed acts of genocide, among other items.

“However, the Court found that Myanmar did not directly and publicly incite the commission of genocide by private persons against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State,” the ruling states, referring to where the Rohingya lived in Myanmar.

The ICJ ordered the country to immediately cease all ongoing violations, take steps to investigate all persons suspected of committing acts of genocide, ensure that acts of genocide do not continue and adopt measures to bring restitution to the Rohingya. It has given the country two years to report back to the court on these restitution efforts.

The world court stated that Myanmar’s military, police and border guards killed around 10,000 Rohingya civilians in incidents involving mass shootings, sexual violence and arson. These attacks drove more than 810,000 Rohingya out of Rakhine and into Bangladesh as refugees.

ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said nine judges voted in favor of the ruling and six objected, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The decision comes seven years after Gambia, a largely Muslim country, filed the case. It’s the fourth time that the world court has ruled that a country met the legal threshold to prove genocide since the Nazi Holocaust and the first time that a state has been held responsible, according to Reuters .

Myanmar, which is in the midst of a civil war, has previously denied accusations of genocide.

International law has faced criticism in recent years after South Africa filed its case against Israel , accusing it of committing genocide on Palestinians in Gaza during the nation’s retribution campaign — sparked by a Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023.

The ICJ ordered Israel in a 13-2 ruling to cease its military operation in May 2024, but Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to continue until there was “complete victory” over Hamas. Israeli officials have denied South Africa’s accusation of genocide, with the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) at the time telling the world court to “ go to hell ” after the ruling.

The world court is limited in how it carries out its orders. Russia ignored a 2022 ruling to stop its invasion of Ukraine, and the U.S. refused the ICJ’s 1986 decision to pay Nicaragua war reparations after the ICJ ruled that the U.S. violated international law.

articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy heads to the Supreme Judicial Court Thursday with her double jeopardy appeal before jury selection in her March retrial begins.
articles.body: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mom accused of murdering her three young children while their father was out running errands in 2023, scored a small legal victory when her appeal was referred to the state's Supreme Judicial Court Thursday, experts say. Earlier this week, Clancy's attorneys filed an appeal of Judge William Sullivan's denial of their motion to dismiss on double jeopardy grounds with Justice Elizabeth Dewar. Dewar referred the case to the full court Thursday, setting briefing deadlines next month and oral arguments for January. Outside the appeal, jury selection in Clancy's retrial is scheduled to begin March 29. "This is a small win for the defense," said Jack Lu, a retired Massachusetts judge and legal scholar who has been following the case. He said the appeal could "unravel" future trials. "Look at it from a common sense perspective, the defendant’s position would interfere with jury deliberations in future cases and presents an unworkable framework for handling deliberating juror complaints." The first trial ended with a hung jury Sept. 4 after a week of deliberations. With a single holdout juror voting to find her guilty, her defense argues that he should have been dismissed and replaced with an alternate after the foreperson accused him of failing to follow the law on "reasonable doubt." articles.title: Hillary Clinton: Xi, Putin play Trump ‘like a child’s guitar’
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin play President Trump “like a child’s guitar.” “All [Trump] cares about, the best I can tell, is looking like he belongs in the company of Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, both of whom he’s going to meet with, together,”…
articles.body:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin play President Trump “like a child’s guitar.”

“All [Trump] cares about, the best I can tell, is looking like he belongs in the company of Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, both of whom he’s going to meet with, together,” Clinton said in a Wednesday episode of the “High Stakes” podcast with journalist Kara Swisher.

“I mean, these two men play him like a child’s guitar,” she added. “It is pathetic.”

Trump, Xi and Putin issued a four-point “ peace declaration ” in the wake of a trilateral summit in China on Thursday. Trump has had notably warm relationships with the leaders of the two U.S. adversaries.

The three leaders discussed United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court and nuclear conflict, according to all three countries.

The peace declaration says that with their status as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, the countries are “committed to promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges” and intend to plan to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”

Trump greeted Putin as a “friend” on Thursday as the two arrived for a meeting.

“Who is he? He’s my friend.” Trump is heard saying after walking into a room with his Russian counterpart.

Earlier this week, the president told reporters he believed the Russian president was “backing down a bit” in the war in Ukraine, which will hit the five-year mark in February.

“I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said. “I think he’s backing down. I think he’d like to, frankly, I think he’d like to see it finished.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.
